I am 76 years old and have farmed this land in Quzhou for 40 years. My family has seven mouths to feed, and my sons help with the heavy work now, though I still make the decisions. With 10.1 mu of good flat land and a well for irrigation, I know this soil well. I always plant wheat in autumn and follow it with maize right after the June harvest — that is the only way to get two crops from this land in one year. For the winter wheat, I will plough the field after the autumn corn harvest, spread my fertilizer, and sow an improved wheat variety that I have used for years because it withstands the cold and gives steady grain. I will irrigate four times: before winter freeze, at green-up, at jointing, and once more when the grain is filling. Wheat needs water at those key moments or the yield drops. For the summer maize, I will plant hybrid seed immediately after cutting the wheat, without tilling again — there is no time to waste in June, and the less I disturb the soil, the better moisture I keep. I will irrigate the maize twice, once when it is knee-high and again at flowering, because July rains can be unreliable. I use my fertilizers generously — nitrogen gives the green growth, phosphorus helps the roots, and potassium keeps the stalks strong. Two sprays on each crop keep the weeds and bugs under control. I expect my wheat to give around 480 jin per mu and the maize around 550 jin per mu if the weather cooperates. That is enough to feed my household and leave some grain to sell.
